title: Plan for the pupils and the school day
focus: Define the year groups, meal numbers and length of each lunch period, then assess whether delivery, a staffed line or another operating model fits the school. Menus and portions need to be reviewed with the responsible school team, alongside dietary information and the required documentation. Consider how pupils receive meals and how service is supervised. The proposal should identify responsibilities for facilities, equipment and communication before an ongoing arrangement is agreed.

sections.title: Plan the school week before the first menu
paragraphs: Build the programme around the timetable pupils actually follow. Record the start and finish of each lunch sitting, the year groups using the dining area and the expected number of meals. Include shorter school days, examinations, trips and other changes that may affect ordering or service during the term.

Decide how meals will be requested and who confirms the final daily order. Some schools collect choices in advance; others need a service counter with an agreed selection. The proposal should explain how each approach affects preparation, portions and the speed of collection. Avoid assuming the full school roll will equal daily meal uptake.

Agree the responsibilities of the school and culinary team at each stage. Receiving, meal identification, supervision and clearance need named owners. A simple written process helps teachers, administration staff and the service team understand the same plan, particularly when someone covers an absence or a timetable changes at short notice.

sections.title: Keep the menu cycle clear for staff and families
paragraphs: A rotating school menu should be easy to understand and practical to deliver. Share the year groups, school food policy and dietary requirements before discussing individual dishes. The school reviews the proposed cycle, portions and ingredient information before it is communicated to families or used for orders.

Allergy requirements need a specific assessment of the proposed kitchen and service arrangements. Agree how approved meals will be identified and who can authorise a substitution. Serving staff should have access to the current information rather than relying on memory or a previous menu version. Any unresolved requirement needs attention before service is confirmed.

Feedback can improve the programme when it is gathered consistently. Ask about dishes pupils enjoyed, portions returned and the clarity of the ordering process. Review changes with the designated school contact so variety develops within the approved menu and policy, with families receiving the appropriate updated information.

sections.title: Make the lunch sitting work in practice
paragraphs: Walk through the route from classroom arrival to tray return. Pupils need a clear way to collect meals and reach their seats, while the service team needs room to replenish without blocking the queue. The number of collection points should reflect the time available and the layout of the hall.

Confirm what the school provides, including tables, service equipment, washing facilities and waste arrangements. If meals are delivered, identify the receiving area and how they move to the dining room. These details belong in the operating plan alongside the menu; they affect how calmly a busy lunch period runs.

Use any trial sitting to review the whole process. Record arrival time, collection time, dietary handovers and clearance, then agree practical adjustments. The aim is a repeatable lunch routine that fits the school day and gives pupils time to eat without requiring staff to solve the same problems each afternoon.
